## The whole setup, in three steps

You do not need a terminal for any of this. If you do not know what a terminal
is, good — you will not be asked to open one.

1. **Install R** — download, double-click, Next, Next, Finish. [Where →](#install-r)
2. **Install RStudio** — same. [Where →](#install-rstudio)
3. **Open RStudio and paste one line** into the *Console* — the pane at the
   bottom left, the one with the `>` prompt — then press Enter:

```r
source("https://sbd-26-27.netlify.app/materials/setup.R")
```

That line installs every course package you are missing, creates a project
folder for the course, and ends with a plain-words report of what it did. It
takes a few minutes the first time. Running it again later is harmless.

If the report ends with ✓ on every line, **you are done** and the rest of this
page is reference. If a line starts with `!`, it tells you what to do next.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**This is for your own machine, not for the exam.** Exams are sat on the computer-lab
machines, which already have R and every course package installed — see
[Assessment](syllabus.qmd#assessment). Set your laptop up so you can practise on it;
you are never asked to bring it to an exam.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Stuck after twenty minutes? Use the browser instead

[**Posit Cloud**](https://posit.cloud/) is RStudio running in a browser tab —
nothing to install, free for what this course needs. Sign up, *New Project*,
and paste the same `source(...)` line into its Console. Your laptop's problem
stops being your problem. Come to [office hours](office-hours.qmd) and we fix
the laptop with no deadline hanging over it.
:::

## Install R {#install-r}

R is the *engine*; RStudio, next section, is the car around it. You install them separately, and you need both.

The course targets **R 4.6.x or newer**. Check what you have:

```r
R.version.string
```

Go to [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/) and follow **Download R
for** your system. It is an ordinary installer: download, open, keep the defaults.

The one step that genuinely trips people up is on a Mac, where CRAN offers two
builds. **Apple silicon (arm64)** is any Mac from the M1 onwards — that is every
MacBook sold since late 2020. **Intel (x86_64)** is older. If you are not sure:
Apple menu → *About This Mac*; if the chip line says *Apple M-something*, take
arm64. Install the wrong one and packages fail with errors that look like
something else entirely.

On **Windows**: click *base*, then the big download link at the top. The
installer asks for administrator rights — on a locked-down work laptop, sort
that out before the lab, not during it.

On **Linux**: follow CRAN's page for your distribution rather than your
distribution's own `r-base` package, which is usually several versions behind.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## If you are comfortable in a terminal: rig

[rig](https://github.com/r-lib/rig), the R Installation Manager, installs R with
one command and picks the right build for your machine — no arm64/Intel
question. Entirely optional; the installer above does the same job.

**macOS**

```bash
brew tap r-lib/rig
brew trust r-lib/rig
brew install --cask rig
```

**Windows**

```powershell
winget install posit.rig
```

**Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)**

```bash
sudo curl -L https://rig.r-pkg.org/deb/rig.gpg -o /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/rig.gpg
sudo sh -c 'echo "deb http://rig.r-pkg.org/deb rig main" > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/rig.list'
sudo apt update
sudo apt install r-rig
```

Then, on any OS:

```bash
rig add release      # install the current R release
rig default release  # make it the one that starts by default
rig list             # see what you have
```

When R 4.7 lands mid-semester, `rig add release` again. Old versions stay installed side by side, so nothing you wrote in October stops working in December.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## If a package install ever fails while compiling

Most packages arrive precompiled. A few build from source, and then you need a compiler:

- macOS: `xcode-select --install`
- Windows: [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/), matched to your R version
- Linux: `sudo apt install build-essential gfortran`

Do this only when an install actually fails with a compilation error — not preemptively.
:::

## Install RStudio {#install-rstudio}

R by itself has no user interface worth the name. RStudio is an **IDE** — editor, console, plots, environment and files in one window — and it is what we use in class and what the lab machines run.

Download **RStudio Desktop** (free, open source) from [posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). Take the installer for your OS and keep the default settings. From then on you open RStudio, never R directly: RStudio starts R for you.

The company behind it used to be called RStudio as well; since 2023 it is **Posit**, because the product line now covers Python too. The IDE kept its name.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What about Positron?

Posit also ships [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/), a newer IDE built on the VS Code core with first-class R *and* Python support. It is genuinely good, and Posit maintains both.

For this course, use RStudio. Every demo, every screenshot below and every lab machine is RStudio, and in an exam room you do not want to be translating menu locations. If you already live in Positron, keep it — just know that when a lecture says "the Environment pane is over there", you are on your own.
:::

## Settings that matter {#settings-that-matter}

Open the preferences: `RStudio > Settings` (`⌘ ,`) on macOS, `Tools > Global Options` (`Ctrl ,`) on Windows.

Three changes, and the first one is the important one.

### 1. Stop restoring your last session

In `General > Basic`, untick everything starting with **Restore**:

- Restore most recently opened project at startup
- Restore previously open source documents at startup
- Restore `.RData` into workspace at startup

And set **Save workspace to .RData on exit** to **Never**.

![](images/setup/00_rstudio_preferences_basic.png)

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
This feels backwards — why throw away your work every time? Because a restored workspace makes your code *look* like it works when it does not. An object you created an hour ago and then deleted from the script is still sitting in memory; your script runs, and it will not run on anyone else's machine, including yours next week. Starting from a clean slate means the script is the only source of truth. This single setting removes most reproducibility bugs you would otherwise spend the semester chasing.
:::

### 2. Editing

In `Code > Editing`, tick at least the first five options — especially **Auto-indent code after paste**. Indentation is the cheapest readability you will ever get.

![](images/setup/01_rstudio_preferences_editing.png)

### 3. Display

In `Display`, tick the first three. **Highlight selected line** earns its keep as soon as your scripts get long.

![](images/setup/02_rstudio_preferences_display.png)

Then go to `Appearance` and pick a theme you like. No right answer here, and a dark theme does not make the models better.

![](images/setup/03_rstudio_preferences_appearance.png)

## R packages {#r-packages}

Most of what makes R useful is not loaded when R starts — it lives in **packages**. A package bundles functions, help files and datasets around one job. "Base R" is just the set of functions you get for free at startup.

Two steps, and people mix them up constantly:

```r
install.packages("dplyr")   # downloads it onto your computer — once, ever
library(dplyr)              # loads it into this session — every session
```

Installing puts the files on disk. Loading makes the functions callable *now*. Quotation marks are required for `install.packages()` and optional for `library()`.

Install several at once by passing a vector:

```r
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "glmnet"))
```

### Course packages {#course-packages}

The `source(...)` line at the top of this page installs exactly this list, and
only the ones you are missing. This is what it runs, so you can see there is
nothing hidden in it:

```r
install.packages(c(
  # data manipulation and graphics
  "tidyverse",     # dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr and friends
  "here",          # sane file paths, see below
  "skimr",         # one-line data summaries

  # Module 1 — regression, regularisation, forecasting
  "glmnet",        # Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net
  "survival",      # survival models
  "fable",         # tidy forecasting
  "feasts",        # time series features and decomposition
  "tsibble",       # time series as tidy data
  "forecast",      # ARIMA and classic forecasting

  # Module 2 — unsupervised learning and machine learning
  "factoextra",    # PCA and clustering visualisation
  "FactoMineR",    # PCA and correspondence analysis
  "cluster",       # k-means, hierarchical clustering, silhouettes
  "rpart",         # decision trees
  "rpart.plot",    # readable tree plots
  "ranger",        # random forests
  "xgboost",       # gradient boosting
  "nnet",          # neural networks
  "iml",           # interpretability: PDP, LIME, feature importance

  # datasets from the textbook
  "ISLR2"
))
```

Check it worked:

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(glmnet)
sessionInfo()
```

If `sessionInfo()` prints without an error, you are set.

### Updating

```r
update.packages(ask = FALSE)
```

R, RStudio and packages update **independently of each other**. Updating RStudio does not update R. This is the single most common source of "it worked yesterday": a package built for a newer R than the one you are running. Start a fresh session after updating anything.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Installing from GitHub

Not everything is on CRAN. Development versions usually live on GitHub:

```r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("user/repo")
```

Newer features, fewer guarantees. Fine for exploring, not what you want the night before an exam.
:::

## Start a project properly {#start-a-project-properly}

Do not work in loose scripts scattered across your Desktop. Make one **RStudio Project** for this course.

If you ran the `source(...)` line, **this is already done**: it created
`sbd_26_27` in your home folder with `data/`, `scripts/` and `output/` inside,
and a project file. Open it with `File > Open Project`, pick
`sbd_26_27/sbd_26_27.Rproj`, and skip to [why it matters](#why-the-project-matters-file-paths).

To make one by hand instead:

1. `File > New Project`

   ![](images/setup/00_r_project_file_menu.png)

2. **New Directory**

   ![](images/setup/01_r_project_new_directory.png)

3. **New Project**

   ![](images/setup/02_r_project_new_project.png)

4. Name it — `sbd_26_27` works — and choose where it lives.

   ![](images/setup/04_r_project_directory_name.png)

5. RStudio opens a fresh session with that folder as the working directory.

   ![](images/setup/05_r_project_new_session.png)

Inside it, make three folders: `data/`, `scripts/`, `output/`.

### Why the project matters: file paths

With a Project, you never write a path like `/Users/yourname/Desktop/stuff/data.csv` again. That path exists on exactly one computer on Earth. Use `here()` instead:

```r
library(here)
here()                            # the project root, whoever is running it
dat <- read_csv(here("data", "bikeshare.csv"))
```

`here()` finds the project root by looking for the `.Rproj` file, so the same line works on your laptop, on mine, and on the lab machines — which is where the exam happens.

## Python {#python}

**Optional, and the only part of this page that uses a terminal.** A few labs
show Python alongside R so you can see the same method in both ecosystems. The
exam is in R. If the commands below mean nothing to you, skip this section
entirely — you lose nothing that is examined.

If you have never installed Python, do not install it from python.org and do not fight your system Python.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### uv (recommended)

[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) installs Python and manages the environment, fast, without touching anything else on your machine.

```bash
# macOS / Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Windows PowerShell
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Then, inside your course folder:

```bash
uv init sbd-python
cd sbd-python
uv add pandas scikit-learn statsmodels pymc matplotlib seaborn jupyter
uv run jupyter lab
```

### Anaconda

If you prefer a click-through installer, get the [Anaconda Distribution](https://www.anaconda.com/download). It ships Python, the scientific stack and Jupyter in one go — several gigabytes, but nothing to configure.

Once installed, open Anaconda Navigator and launch JupyterLab.

:::

The packages we use:

| Package | What for |
|---|---|
| `pandas` | data frames |
| `scikit-learn` | trees, forests, boosting, clustering, PCA |
| `statsmodels` | regression and time series, closer to the R output you will recognise |
| `pymc` | Bayesian models |
| `matplotlib`, `seaborn` | plots |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
You are not expected to be fluent in both languages. The exam's coding part is in **R**. Python appears so you can see that the same method looks different in two ecosystems — useful the day a colleague hands you a `scikit-learn` pipeline.
:::

## When something breaks {#troubleshooting}

**`there is no package called 'x'`** — you loaded before installing. Run `install.packages("x")`.

**`could not find function "f"`** — the package is installed but not loaded in *this* session. Run `library(...)`.

**Install fails with compilation errors** — you need the build tools: `xcode-select --install` on macOS, [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) on Windows.

**`cannot open file 'data.csv'`** — a working directory problem. Open the Project, then use `here()`.

**A package refuses to install: "is not available for this version of R"** — your R is too old. Check `R.version.string`; if it starts with anything below 4.6, [reinstall R from CRAN](#install-r) — the installer replaces the old one. This bites people who installed R for a bachelor course three years ago and never touched it again.

**It worked yesterday** — check `R.version.string` and whether you updated something. Restart R with `⌘⇧F10` / `Ctrl+Shift+F10` and run the script top to bottom in a clean session.

Still stuck? Bring the failing script and the exact error text to [office hours](office-hours.qmd) — a file beats a screenshot, and a screenshot beats a description.
